That leaves us with Carl, a grumpy homebody voiced by Ed Asner, who makes WALL-E seem like a chatterbox. And he is one of the main characters. No, I did not hear anyone asking when the dancing penguins were going to appear, but I would wager someone was thinking it. Watch a preview of *Up* ».

There are zeppelins, old-time explorers, and talking dogs—a whole pack of dogs, in fact. Dogs that serve wine, play cards, and fly biplanes.

(CNN) — At first, Pixar’s 10th full-length feature, “Up,” seems as though it may turn into something rather melancholy.

The film centers on Carl, a cranky elderly man, as he deals with the relentless cheerfulness of Russell, a young boy. Of course, there is nothing inherently wrong with an animated movie aiming for an emotional response. Still, it is easy to imagine younger viewers growing uneasy during the film’s lively opening sequence. Roughly five minutes in, the adventurous children Carl and Ellie suddenly become newlyweds, and then an older married couple. Viewers watch them age, bend, and slow down, while their early hopes of grand exploration give way to domestic happiness and the routines of home.

Ellie longs to have a child, but she is unable to. The money the couple sets aside for their dream trip is repeatedly drained by emergencies and household setbacks, until eventually time runs out — for Ellie, at least.

That leaves Carl, a sour, reclusive widower voiced by Ed Asner, whose silence makes WALL-E seem talkative by comparison. And Carl is one of the central figures. No, I did not hear anyone asking aloud when the dancing penguins would arrive, but I suspect someone in the audience may have wondered.

Those doubts, however, turn out to be misplaced. In terms of spectacle and excitement, “Up” comes through. It may not offer penguins exactly, but it provides far more than the flying house shown in the advertisements. The movie includes a legendary, brightly colored bird — possibly a snipe, possibly not — named Kevin, who has a fondness for candy bars. It also features zeppelins, vintage adventurers, and talking dogs — an entire pack of them, actually. These dogs serve wine, play cards, and pilot biplanes.

Then there is Russell, a plump Boy Scout — or, as the movie calls him, a “Wilderness Explorer” — who appears on Carl’s porch at the worst possible moment. Carl is trying to escape, and he does so by sending his house into the air with the help of thousands of balloons. How could he have known Russell was nearby?

“Up” is not flawless. The dogs’ comic antics sometimes feel closer to “Beverly Hills Chihuahua” than what audiences might expect from Pixar, a studio usually more careful about bending the rules of nature merely for easy jokes. Still, if the muttering canines entertain children, that is no small thing.

The film is far stronger when it develops the bond between Carl and Russell as they drift high above the world. Russell is openhearted, eager, innocent, and endlessly enthusiastic, even when his attempts to help go wrong. In many ways, he reflects the child Carl once was — though Carl himself is too closed off to see it. Rather than taking in what is around him, Carl is obsessed with bringing his beloved house to the location he believes represents his final dream: the lost realm of Paradise Falls.

The sight of Carl heroically hauling his house through jungles and across mountains will resonate with anyone who has ever had a mortgage.

Written by Bob Petersen and directed by Petersen and Pete Docter, both longtime Pixar figures, “Up” combines metaphor, adventure, and playful imagination. The mix is not quite as seamless as in Pixar’s finest films, but the movie’s buoyant spirit is hard to resist. Russell, voiced by Jordan Nagai, is especially winning. Although he is only 8 years old and already carries emotional burdens of his own, he is deeply kind and generous — the sort of child who reflects well on children in general.

Shown in 3-D where available, “Up” avoids overusing stereoscopic tricks. Instead, it makes effective use of depth in a series of thrilling cliffside moments and aerial battles.

Funny, moving, and bursting with vitality, “Up” easily ranks among the strongest films of the year so far. See it with someone who matters to you.

“Up” is rated PG and has a running time of 96 minutes.

In just a few minutes, it follows Carl and Ellie from their childhood dreams of adventure through their marriage, their shared hopes, their disappointments, and finally Ellie’s death. By the time Carl is shown living alone in old age, the film has already created a deep sense of love, loss, and nostalgia.

His sadness and frustration are rooted in genuine grief, and his journey becomes as much emotional as it is physical.

Carl’s decision to attach thousands of balloons to his house and fly away transforms the story from a quiet portrait of loneliness into a colorful journey across the skies. The film balances its sadness with playful energy, ensuring that its emotional weight never overwhelms its sense of wonder.

The adventure is filled with fantastical elements that give *Up* its distinctive charm. There is the unforgettable image of Carl’s house floating beneath a massive cluster of balloons, as well as a rare, brightly colored bird named Kevin, mysterious explorers, zeppelins, and a pack of dogs equipped with collars that allow them to speak. Pixar’s *Up* is, at first glance, a bright and whimsical adventure about a house carried into the sky by thousands of balloons. Yet what makes the film so striking is how quickly it reveals itself to be about much heavier matters: aging, grief, disappointment, and the painful distance between the life one imagined and the life one actually lived. Rather than opening with easy jokes or immediate action, the film begins with an unexpectedly somber sequence that traces the relationship between Carl Fredricksen and his wife, Ellie. In just a few minutes, it shows childhood dreams, marriage, illness, loss, and the quiet sorrow of growing old alone. It is a bold beginning for a family film, and it gives the rest of the story an emotional weight that never fully disappears.

The central figure, Carl, is not the usual animated hero. He is elderly, stubborn, lonely, and burdened by regret. His decision to tie balloons to his house and fly away to South America is both a comic fantasy and an act of desperation. He wants to fulfill a promise he made to Ellie, but he also wants to escape a world that has moved on without him. This mixture of sadness and absurdity is typical of the film’s unusual tone. *Up* is full of colorful sights, eccentric characters, talking dogs, and chase sequences, but beneath the adventure is a serious concern with how people carry the past with them.

The arrival of Russell, the enthusiastic young Wilderness Explorer who accidentally joins Carl’s journey, gives the film much of its warmth and humor. Their relationship develops in familiar odd-couple fashion: Carl is impatient and closed off, while Russell is eager, talkative, and emotionally open. Even so, the bond between them works because it is rooted in need rather than convenience. Russell needs attention and guidance; Carl needs to rediscover the possibility of caring for someone in the present rather than living entirely in memory. Through Russell, the film gently suggests that honoring the dead does not mean refusing to keep living.

The adventure elements are imaginative and often delightful. The floating house is one of Pixar’s most memorable images, combining childlike fantasy with emotional symbolism. Paradise Falls, the great destination of Ellie and Carl’s dream, is rendered with a sense of wonder that recalls old adventure serials and travel fantasies. The film also introduces broad comic figures such as Dug, the dog whose collar translates his thoughts into speech, and Kevin, the exotic bird pursued by the villain. These touches make the movie more accessible to younger viewers and keep it from becoming too heavy.

At times, however, the comedy can feel uneven. Some of the talking-dog humor and action-oriented villainy seem less inspired than the film’s quieter emotional material. The shift from the devastating intimacy of the opening to the more conventional adventure plot may initially feel jarring. There are moments when *Up* appears to be two different films stitched together: one a deeply moving reflection on loss and memory, the other a lively cartoon expedition filled with slapstick and spectacle. But the film largely succeeds because the adventure is never completely detached from Carl’s inner life. His journey is not simply to a faraway place; it is toward acceptance.

What is most impressive about *Up* is its willingness to trust a family audience with complicated feelings. It does not treat children as incapable of understanding sadness, nor does it offer adults only nostalgia and visual polish. Instead, it blends melancholy and playfulness in a way that feels honest. The film recognizes that joy and sorrow often coexist, and that even the most colorful adventure can begin from loneliness.

By the end, *Up* turns its unusual seriousness into its greatest strength. The balloons, the flying house, the strange creatures, and the comic side characters all serve a story about learning to let go without forgetting. Though one might initially doubt whether such a somber foundation can support a family adventure, the film proves that emotional depth and imaginative spectacle can enrich one another. *Up* is not merely charming or inventive; it is moving because it understands that life’s great adventures are shaped as much by loss as by discovery.

**Review: Pixar’s “Up” soars on humor, heartbreak and high-flying adventure**

Pixar’s 2009 film **“Up”** begins with one of the most emotionally affecting sequences in modern animation: a near-wordless montage tracing the life of Carl Fredricksen and his wife, Ellie, from childhood dreams of exploration to marriage, disappointment, aging and loss. In just a few minutes, the film establishes a lifetime of love and regret — and gives its floating-house adventure real emotional weight.

The story follows **Carl** (voiced by Ed Asner), a gruff widower who refuses to let go of the home he shared with Ellie. Facing eviction and a move to a retirement facility, Carl ties thousands of balloons to his house and lifts off toward **Paradise Falls**, the South American destination he and Ellie always dreamed of visiting. But he soon discovers an accidental stowaway: **Russell**, an eager, chatty Wilderness Explorer who needs one final merit badge for “assisting the elderly.”

Their journey introduces some of Pixar’s most memorable comic creations, including **Dug**, a lovable dog whose special collar translates his thoughts into speech, and **Kevin**, a giant, colorful bird being hunted by famed explorer **Charles Muntz**. Muntz, once Carl’s childhood hero, becomes the film’s antagonist — a reminder that dreams curdled by obsession can turn dangerous.

For all its melancholy, “Up” is also frequently funny. Much of the humor comes from Carl and Russell’s odd-couple dynamic: Carl is stubborn and impatient, while Russell is earnest, needy and impossible to ignore. Dug’s distracted dog logic — especially his sudden fixation on “squirrel!” — adds a lighter, almost slapstick rhythm to the film’s heavier themes.

Visually, “Up” is bright, expressive and expansive, with the floating house providing one of Pixar’s most iconic images. The **3-D presentation** enhances the sense of height, depth and motion without overwhelming the story. Rather than relying on gimmicks, the effect supports the film’s central wonder: a modest house drifting through vast skies toward an impossible dream.

The result is a film that works as both a comic adventure and a meditation on grief, aging and learning to keep living after loss. “Up” may be marketed as family entertainment, but its opening and emotional payoff speak just as powerfully to adults.

**Verdict:** Pixar’s “Up” is funny, beautiful and deeply moving — a rare animated adventure that truly earns its tears as well as its laughs.

# *Up* Review: Pixar’s Soaring Adventure Finds Its Greatest Heights in the Heart

Pixar’s *Up* is the kind of animated film that begins with a fantastical image—a house lifted into the sky by thousands of balloons—and somehow turns it into one of the most emotionally grounded stories the studio has ever told. Rated PG, the film balances family-friendly adventure with unusually mature themes: grief, regret, aging, loneliness, and the quiet ways people learn to begin again. It is bright, funny, and thrilling, but its real power lies in its tenderness.

At the center of the film is Carl Fredricksen, a retired balloon salesman whose life has narrowed to the edges of his old home. Carl is gruff, stubborn, and resistant to change, but the film quickly shows that his bitterness is not simple crankiness. It is sorrow hardened into habit. His beloved wife, Ellie, is gone, and with her went the shared dream that defined much of his life: an adventure to Paradise Falls in South America.

The film’s opening sequence, which traces Carl and Ellie’s life together, remains one of Pixar’s finest achievements. In just a few minutes, largely without dialogue, it captures childhood wonder, romantic devotion, disappointment, illness, and loss. It is moving not because it is manipulative, but because it understands how a life is made up of ordinary moments: painting a mailbox, saving coins in a jar, dancing in a living room, sitting side by side through the years. Ellie may be absent for much of the film’s present-day action, but her presence gives *Up* its emotional architecture.

Carl’s decision to tie balloons to his house and fly away is both absurd and deeply understandable. It is an act of rebellion, an escape, and a tribute. He is not merely chasing a destination; he is trying to preserve the last physical and emotional connection to Ellie. The image of the house floating above the city is whimsical, but it carries enormous symbolic weight. Carl is lifting his memories into the air, refusing to let the world tear them down.

Of course, no Pixar adventure can remain entirely solitary. Enter Russell, an eager young Wilderness Explorer who accidentally becomes Carl’s traveling companion. Russell is chatty, earnest, and hilariously ill-equipped for the expedition he so badly wants to complete. His goal is simple: earn his final merit badge for assisting the elderly. But beneath his comic enthusiasm is a child’s longing for attention and approval. His relationship with Carl develops into the film’s emotional second act, gradually transforming from irritation into reluctant partnership and, finally, chosen family.

The dynamic between Carl and Russell is one of the film’s great pleasures. Carl represents a man trapped in the past; Russell represents a future Carl never expected to care about. Their comic timing is sharp, but the writing avoids reducing either character to a type. Carl is not just a “grumpy old man,” and Russell is not just an “annoying kid.” They are two lonely people who do not initially realize how much they need each other.

Once the house reaches the wilds near Paradise Falls, *Up* shifts into a more traditional adventure mode, introducing a colorful collection of supporting characters. Chief among them is Kevin, the giant tropical bird Russell names with full confidence before discovering that Kevin is female. Kevin is a triumph of visual comedy: gangly, expressive, ridiculous, and oddly majestic. She brings kinetic energy to the film, serving as both comic relief and a catalyst for the story’s moral choices.

Then there are the talking dogs, one of the film’s funniest inventions. Equipped with collars that translate their thoughts into speech, the dogs are a perfect Pixar gag: simple, clever, and endlessly rewarding. Dug, the sweet and loyal golden retriever, is especially memorable, with his instant affection and famously distractible attention span. The dogs’ dialogue captures the essence of canine behavior with delightful accuracy—devotion, insecurity, territorial pride, and sudden obsession with squirrels.

The humor surrounding the talking dogs helps lighten a story that might otherwise feel too heavy for younger audiences. That balance is part of what makes the film’s PG rating appropriate. *Up* contains moments of peril, sadness, and emotional intensity, including scenes involving loss and danger, but it remains accessible to family audiences. The rating reflects a film that is gentle in spirit but not afraid to acknowledge that life can be painful.

The villain of *Up*, Charles Muntz, is also tied to the film’s deeper themes. Once Carl’s childhood hero, Muntz has become consumed by pride and obsession. He is a cautionary mirror for Carl: a man who has allowed a dream to curdle into isolation and cruelty. Through Muntz, the film asks an important question: What happens when a dream becomes more important than people? Carl’s journey is, in part, learning that honoring Ellie does not mean clinging to the past so tightly that he misses the life still in front of him.

Visually, *Up* is magnificent. The contrast between Carl’s square, heavy design and Russell’s round, buoyant presence tells us everything about them before they speak. The floating house, with its explosion of colored balloons, remains one of Pixar’s most iconic images. Paradise Falls is rendered with sweeping beauty, evoking old adventure serials while still feeling like a storybook landscape. The animation is stylized rather than photorealistic, but its emotional truth is precise.

Michael Giacchino’s score is essential to the film’s impact. Ellie’s theme, delicate and nostalgic, threads through the movie like a memory Carl cannot put down. The music is wistful without becoming sentimental, adventurous without overwhelming the intimacy of the story. It helps *Up* move gracefully between comedy and heartbreak, often within the same scene.

What makes *Up* extraordinary is not merely that it makes viewers cry early and laugh often. It is that the film understands adventure in a more profound way than its premise suggests. Adventure is not only crossing oceans, climbing cliffs, or discovering rare creatures. It is also loving someone, losing someone, caring for someone new, and having the courage to keep living after the life you planned has ended.

Carl’s transformation is beautifully handled. He does not forget Ellie, nor does the film suggest that grief can be neatly resolved. Instead, he comes to understand Ellie’s love as permission, not a prison. The revelation that she considered their life together to be her great adventure is devastating and liberating. It reframes everything Carl has been carrying. His obligation is not to finish an old dream exactly as imagined, but to live in the spirit of the love that created it.

Russell, Kevin, Dug, and even the chaotic talking dogs all help pull Carl back into the world. They are not distractions from Ellie’s memory; they are the continuation of what Ellie gave him. By the end, Carl’s house—once a shrine to what he lost—has become less important than the relationships he chooses to protect.

As a work of family entertainment, *Up* is funny, inventive, and visually dazzling. As a film about grief and renewal, it is remarkably wise. Pixar has often excelled at finding adult emotions inside child-friendly stories, but *Up* stands among the studio’s most affecting achievements because it treats sorrow with respect while still insisting on joy.

It is a film about a flying house, a lonely old man, a persistent boy, a rare bird named Kevin, and dogs whose collars say exactly what they are thinking. But more than that, *Up* is about the courage to let go without forgetting, and to discover that life’s next adventure may arrive uninvited, wearing a merit badge sash and knocking on the front door.

**Rating: 4.5 out of 5 stars**

# Pixar’s “Up” Soars on Emotion, Even When Its Canine Comedy Loses Altitude

In a summer-movie landscape often crowded with noise, spectacle and easy laughs, Pixar’s *Up* arrives with a quieter headline: an animated film about grief, aging and adventure can still feel like an event.

Directed by Pete Docter and Bob Peterson, *Up* begins with one of Pixar’s most celebrated sequences — a nearly wordless montage tracing the life of Carl Fredricksen and his wife, Ellie. Their love story, shown through small domestic moments and unrealized dreams, gives the film an emotional foundation before the main adventure even begins. When Carl, now a lonely widower, faces the loss of his home, he ties thousands of balloons to it and lifts off toward South America, hoping to fulfill the journey he and Ellie once imagined.

Complicating that escape is Russell, an eager young Wilderness Explorer who accidentally becomes Carl’s passenger. Together, they land near Paradise Falls, encounter a rare tropical bird named Kevin, and cross paths with Charles Muntz, Carl’s childhood hero turned obsessive adventurer.

The film’s greatest strength is its emotional clarity. Carl’s floating house is more than a whimsical visual; it is a symbol of memory, attachment and the difficulty of moving forward. Pixar balances that weight with bright adventure, turning what could have been a simple journey story into a meditation on letting go.

Not every comic element works equally well. The talking dogs, led by the instantly distracted Dug, provide some of the film’s broadest humor. Dug himself is charming in small doses, especially when his loyalty and simple-hearted affection cut through Carl’s gruffness. But the dog scenes occasionally push the movie toward sillier territory, undercutting the tenderness and tension that make the central story so strong. The pack’s high-tech collars and repeated gags can feel less inspired than the film’s more character-driven comedy.

Russell, however, is a standout. Voiced with warmth and sincerity, he avoids becoming merely a cute sidekick. His optimism, loneliness and need for approval give him surprising depth, and his relationship with Carl becomes the film’s emotional engine. Russell’s presence forces Carl to reengage with the world, not through lectures or sentimentality, but through shared danger, frustration and genuine companionship.

Visually, *Up* is often stunning: a tiny house beneath a mountain of balloons, sweeping South American landscapes, and character designs that turn age, innocence and obsession into instantly readable silhouettes. Michael Giacchino’s score adds another layer of poignancy, especially in the film’s opening and closing movements.

Final recommendation: *Up* is one of Pixar’s most moving achievements — a film that begins with heartbreak, rises on imagination and lands with grace. A few overplayed dog jokes aside, it is a funny, beautiful and deeply humane adventure worth watching for children and adults alike.

Pixar’s **“Up”** is the rare animated family film that feels both grandly adventurous and deeply personal, a helium-bright comedy built around grief, regret, and the fragile persistence of hope. Directed by Pete Docter, the film begins with one of the most celebrated sequences in modern animation: a wordless montage tracing the marriage of Carl and Ellie Fredricksen from childhood dreams to old age, disappointment, illness, and loss. It is elegant, economical, and devastating—more emotionally mature than what many live-action dramas manage in two hours.

At its center is **Ed Asner** as Carl Fredricksen, a widowed balloon salesman whose square body, clenched jaw, and cranky mutterings conceal an ocean of tenderness. Asner’s vocal performance is essential to the film’s success: he makes Carl irritable without making him cruel, wounded without making him sentimental. Opposite him, **Jordan Nagai** gives Russell, the overeager Wilderness Explorer who accidentally joins Carl’s airborne journey, a wonderfully natural comic energy. Russell could have been merely a cute-kid sidekick, but Nagai’s unpolished sincerity gives him an appealing, believable sweetness.

Compared with other animated family films, “Up” stands apart for how boldly it centers an elderly protagonist and treats loss as more than a plot device. Where many family adventures—such as “Shrek,” “Madagascar,” or even lesser studio cartoons of the era—lean heavily on pop-culture jokes and manic pacing, “Up” is more classical in its storytelling. It has the emotional architecture of Pixar’s best work, sitting comfortably alongside **“Toy Story,” “Finding Nemo,”** and **“WALL-E.”** Like “Finding Nemo,” it is about an anxious adult learning to let life in again; like “WALL-E,” it trusts silence and visual storytelling; like “Toy Story,” it finds profound feeling in a simple premise. Yet “Up” is also looser and more whimsical than those films, especially once the story reaches South America and introduces a giant colorful bird, a pack of talking dogs, and the adventurer Charles Muntz.

The film’s second half is more conventional than its opening act, shifting into chase scenes, villainy, and action-comedy. The talking dogs—especially the instantly lovable Dug—are funny and memorable, though their broad humor occasionally pulls the movie away from the melancholy grace that makes the beginning so extraordinary. Still, Pixar balances tones with remarkable skill. The house lifted by balloons is a perfect image: absurd, beautiful, and emotionally precise. It represents Carl’s refusal to let go of the past, and the film’s power lies in showing that love is not betrayed by moving forward.

Visually, “Up” is a triumph of design rather than realism. Carl’s blocky silhouette, Russell’s roundness, the floating Victorian house, and the painterly landscapes all create a world that feels stylized but emotionally true. The use of color is especially expressive: muted grays and browns define Carl’s lonely city life, while the skies and jungles of Paradise Falls burst with storybook vibrancy.

The **3-D effects** are tasteful rather than showy. Unlike animated films that use 3-D mainly to hurl objects at the audience, “Up” uses depth to enhance scale and atmosphere: the floating house drifting across clouds, the vast drop of the cliffs, and the layered jungle environments all gain a pleasing sense of space. It is not essential to appreciating the film, but it adds immersion without becoming distracting. The 3-D supports the storytelling instead of competing with it.

“Up” is funny, visually inventive, and emotionally piercing—a family film that respects children enough to tell them the truth about sorrow, and respects adults enough to remind them that adventure is not only for the young. Its opening may be its masterpiece, but the whole film remains one of Pixar’s most moving achievements.

**Runtime: 96 minutes. Rating: PG.**
